desc:
Houses stand in a row and house i holds nums[i] coins. Every time you rob a house, the police patrol the next gap houses: if you rob house i, you cannot rob any of the houses i + 1, i + 2, ..., i + gap. Houses further away are safe again.

Return the largest total you can rob. With gap = 1 this is the classic House Robber.

For example, for nums = [7, 2, 2, 2, 7] the answer is 16 when gap = 1, 14 when gap = 2 and only 7 when gap = 4.
hints: For gap = 1 you know the recurrence best(i) = max(best(i-1), best(i-2) + nums[i]). Think about how 'i-2' changes when the cooldown is longer.
If you rob house p, the previous robbed house must be at index p - gap - 1 or earlier, so the prefix you can still use has length p - gap.
Let best[i] be the best total using only the first i houses. Then best[i] = max(best[i-1], nums[i-1] + best[max(0, i-1-gap)]). Keep the whole best array, since you look back gap + 1 positions.
editorial: Define best[i] as the maximum total from the first i houses, with best[0] = 0. For house index p = i-1 there are two choices. Skip it: the answer stays best[i-1]. Rob it: the previously robbed house must lie at index ≤ p - gap - 1, so everything before it comes from the first p - gap houses, giving nums[p] + best[max(0, p - gap)].

The answer is best[n]. The recurrence needs random access to an entry gap + 1 steps back, so keep the entire array instead of two rolling variables. That is O(n) time and O(n) space, independent of the gap size.
solution:
def robWithGap(nums, gap):
    n = len(nums)
    best = [0] * (n + 1)
    for i in range(1, n + 1):
        take = nums[i - 1] + best[max(0, i - 1 - gap)]
        best[i] = max(best[i - 1], take)
    return best[n]
